1.title: the word you already say
1.hook: said at good news and bad, all day, at home; the word Sikhs say for God, and it means "wow, the teacher"
1.tomorrow: everyone on the floor, everyone the same meal
1.howItsDone: Sikhs repeat Waheguru in meditation, often slowly with the breath, say it in everyday moments of joy or difficulty, and greet each other with "Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh."

segments.voice: Good news on the phone: Waheguru. Someone stands up after sitting on the floor too long: Waheguru. Hard news, said softer: Waheguru. In many Sikh homes it's said all day long, and hardly ever translated. It turns out to be a name for God built from the smallest word people say when something is bigger than they are.
screen: `GOOD NEWS: WAHEGURU.` → `HARD NEWS: WAHEGURU.` → `HARDLY EVER TRANSLATED.`

segments.voice: Break it in two. Wahe: wow, wonderful, the cry of amazement. Guru: the teacher, the one who leads from darkness into light. So Waheguru is something like: wow, the teacher. Notice what kind of name that is. It isn't a title, like king or judge. It's a reaction. Sikh scripture speaks of a God beyond counting and beyond description, so instead of a description, the name is a response: when words run out, you say wow. That's why the same word fits joy, relief and grief. It isn't reporting how you feel. It's pointing past the feeling, to what's bigger. It's the word Sikhs repeat in meditation, slowly, on the breath. And it's inside the greeting Sikhs trade: Waheguru ji ka Khalsa, Waheguru ji ki fateh. The Khalsa, the community of committed Sikhs, belongs to Waheguru, and so does the victory. Ji is a small word of respect, like dear. So the word you've heard all your life carries a whole idea: wonder isn't only a mood. It's a way of paying attention. And no Punjabi needed here: every word on this path comes with what's inside it.
screen: `WAHE — WOW. GURU — TEACHER.` · `NOT A TITLE. A REACTION.` · `THE SAME WORD FOR JOY AND GRIEF.` · `INSIDE THE SIKH GREETING.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Look at something near you: your hand, a window, a cup. Breathe in and look at it as if you'd never seen one before. On the way out, if you like, let the word go with the breath, aloud or silently: Waheguru. Wow.
Waheguru. Wahe, wow; guru, the teacher. The name Sikhs say for God, made of wonder. First word on your strand.

segments.voice: Your line: wow. It's the whole name, said the way it feels, and now you know what's inside it. See you tomorrow.

story.title: a puzzle in four letters
story.text: The scribe who wrote out the first Sikh scripture as the fifth Guru compiled it, Bhai Gurdas, also wrote poems of his own, and in one of them he takes Waheguru apart letter by letter. Each age of the world, he says, called on God by its own name: Vasudev, Hari, Gobind and Ram. Take the first letter of each, put the four together, and you hear Waheguru. It's one poet's reading, not a dictionary's, and Sikhs still love telling it.

2.title: everyone on the floor, everyone the same meal
2.hook: everyone on the floor, everyone the same meal
2.howItsDone: Gurdwaras run a langar: volunteers cook a simple vegetarian meal and serve it free to anyone, traditionally seated together in rows on the floor.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Waheguru. Wahe, wow; guru, the teacher. Today, a meal plenty of people have eaten sitting on a gurdwara floor.

Next to the Golden Temple in Amritsar there's a kitchen that never closes. Anyone can walk in and eat: no ticket, no questions. People at the temple speak of tens of thousands of meals on an ordinary day. And there are no chairs. A banker sits beside a laborer, a first-time visitor beside a grandmother who's come for sixty years, all on the floor in long rows. Where you sit usually says who you are. Here, it can't.
screen: `A KITCHEN THAT NEVER CLOSES.` → `NO TICKET. NO CHAIRS.` → `LONG ROWS ON THE FLOOR.`

segments.voice: Langar is the free community kitchen, and the meal that comes out of it. Gurdwaras keep one. Tradition traces it to Guru Nanak, who shared food with everyone who came to his town of Kartarpur, and the Gurus after him built it into an institution. Here's why it mattered. In Nanak's Punjab, caste rules decided who could eat with whom, and who could even cook for whom. Eating side by side across those lines could be a scandal. The langar did it on purpose, every day. The row everyone sits in even has its own name: pangat. Three details carry the idea. The floor: nobody sits higher, because there's nothing to sit higher on. The food: simple and vegetarian, so someone of any faith or diet can eat without asking what's in it. And the guest list: there isn't one. Any faith, or none. You sit down, hold out your hands, and someone puts a roti in them. The meal is a teaching you can taste: one God, one row.
screen: `LANGAR — THE KITCHEN AND THE MEAL.` · `EATING ACROSS THE LINES OF CASTE.` · `PANGAT — THE ROW.` · `THE FLOOR, THE FOOD, THE GUEST LIST.`

segments.voice: One breath with the bell. Picture yourself in the row: on your left, someone you'd never usually sit beside; on your right, someone else. Breathe in. As you breathe out, hold out your hands, palms up, the way people do when the roti comes down the row.
Langar. The free kitchen, and the meal where everyone sits in one row and eats the same food. Second word.
Your line: nobody sits higher. That's the whole teaching of the meal, in three words. Day two, done.

story.title: dinner on the highway
story.text: Just before Christmas in 2020, France suddenly closed its border with England, and thousands of truck drivers were stranded in Kent, stuck in their cabs for days. Nobody asked who anyone was. It was langar, served on the side of the road.

3.title: is that a hat?
3.hook: what's under the turban, what the color means, and the plain steel circle on the wrist
3.howItsDone: Many Sikhs keep their hair uncut; men and some women tie a turban fresh each day, others cover their hair with a scarf, and many Sikhs, including some who don't keep the other articles of faith, wear a steel kara on the wrist. Everyone covers their head in the gurdwara.

segments.voice: Yesterday: langar, where nobody sits higher. Today, the questions a lot of Sikhs get asked at school and at work.

Is that a hat? What's under there? Does the color mean something? Sikhs who wear a turban hear these at school, at work and in the airport security line. The real answers are better than most people expect. And there's a second thing that often needs explaining, on the wrist: a plain steel circle.
screen: `IS THAT A HAT?` → `WHAT'S UNDER THERE?` → `AND THE CIRCLE ON THE WRIST.`

segments.voice: Start underneath. Many Sikhs keep their hair uncut all their lives, as a way of accepting the body as it was made. That's kesh. The turban, the dastar or pagg, covers and looks after that hair. So no, it isn't a hat that comes off with the weather. Most who wear one tie it fresh each morning, over hair combed and knotted on top, yards of cloth wrapped layer by layer. Sikh tradition remembers that in the Gurus' world a fine turban marked kings and nobles. The tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh, made it part of his community's identity, so every Sikh who ties one wears a crown, whatever family they come from. The color? For most, simply a choice, or what goes with the day. And not every Sikh wears one: some women do, many cover their hair with a scarf, and Sikhs keep the faith in different ways. If you've cut your hair, you're every bit as welcome on this path. Now the wrist. The kara is a plain steel bracelet: a circle with no beginning and no end, like the one God. Steel, not gold, on purpose. It isn't jewelry. Sikhs often say that when your hand reaches for something, the kara gets there first and asks: should my hand be doing this?
screen: `KESH — HAIR, LEFT AS IT GREW.` · `THE DASTAR — A CROWN YOU TIE.` · `THE COLOR IS USUALLY A CHOICE.` · `THE KARA — STEEL, NOT GOLD.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, sit up and let the crown of your head rise, as if something precious rested there. On the second, touch your wrist, where a kara would sit. On the third, think of one thing your hands will reach for today.
The turban. A crown tied fresh over hair left as it grew, and beside it, the steel kara. Third word.
Your line: a crown you tie yourself. Next time someone asks if it's a hat, that's the short answer. Day three.

4.title: five who said yes
4.hook: the five people dressed alike at the front of the parade, and the day in 1699 they stand in for
4.howItsDone: At every amrit initiation, five initiated Sikhs stand in as the Panj Pyare, and five Sikhs dressed alike lead Nagar Kirtan processions ahead of the Guru Granth Sahib; the Khalsa's founding is celebrated every year at Vaisakhi.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the turban, a crown you tie yourself, and the steel kara. Today, the morning in 1699 that both trace back to.

At the front of a Sikh parade, ahead of the float carrying the scripture, walk five people dressed alike, swords held upright. They aren't security, and they aren't there for show. They're standing in for five people from more than three hundred years ago, who did something nobody in the crowd that day expected.
screen: `FIVE, DRESSED ALIKE, AT THE FRONT.` → `NOT SECURITY. NOT FOR SHOW.` → `STANDING IN FOR FIVE.`

segments.voice: Spring, 1699, at Anandpur in the hills of Punjab. A huge crowd has gathered for the harvest festival, Vaisakhi. The tenth Guru, Guru Gobind Singh, walks out with a drawn sword and asks a question that silences everyone: who will give their head for the faith? One man stands, Daya Ram. The Guru takes him into a tent and comes back out alone. Then he asks again. Four more stand, one at a time. What happened inside that tent, the tellings differ. What they agree on is what came next: all five walked out alive, dressed alike, beside the Guru. They're remembered as the Panj Pyare: panj, five, pyare, beloved. And look who they were. A shopkeeper from Lahore. A farmer from near Delhi. A water-carrier from Puri, on the eastern coast. A cloth printer from Dwarka, in the far west. A barber from Bidar, in the south. Castes that, around them, would never have shared a meal, from homes a thousand miles apart. They became the first of the Khalsa, the community of committed Sikhs: one family. The men took one name, Singh, lion, and Sikh women carry the name Kaur. Two names that rank no one.
screen: `WHO WILL GIVE THEIR HEAD?` · `ALL FIVE WALK OUT ALIVE.` · `FIVE CASTES, FIVE CORNERS OF INDIA.` · `SINGH AND KAUR — ONE FAMILY.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, picture the crowd on the hillside, gone quiet. On the second, picture one person standing up when nobody else will. On the third, sit a little taller yourself, the way someone does when they stand for what they love.
Panj Pyare. The five beloved: strangers from across India who stood up, and walked out one family. Fourth word.
Your line: five strangers, one family. The five at the front of every parade are standing in for them. That's day four.

5.title: the standing prayer
5.hook: the standing prayer; "sarbat da bhala" — the good of all
5.howItsDone: Sikhs stand with palms joined, facing the Guru Granth Sahib, while one person leads the Ardas at the end of services and before important events; it closes by asking for chardi kala and sarbat da bhala, the good of all, and the congregation answers the call "bole so nihal" with "sat sri akal."

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Panj Pyare, five strangers, one family. Today, the prayer that remembers them every time it's said.

End of the service. Someone steps forward, and the whole room rises: palms together, facing the scripture. Plenty of people have stood for it since they were small without knowing what's being said. Then a voice calls out, bole so nihal, and the room shouts back, sat sri akal. Today, what everyone is standing for.
screen: `THE ROOM RISES.` → `PALMS TOGETHER.` → `WHAT IS BEING SAID?`

segments.voice: It's the Ardas. The word comes from Persian, for a petition, a humble request. Sikhs say it standing, facing the Guru Granth Sahib, at the end of services and before anything important: a wedding, a journey, a new home. It has a shape. It opens by remembering the Gurus, one by one, from Nanak on. Then it remembers more: the scripture, the five beloved from yesterday, and the men and women who suffered for their faith. A prayer with a long memory. Then it turns personal. The one leading adds the day's requests: a new baby, a grandmother in the hospital, thanks for a new job. So no two are quite the same. And the end never changes. It asks for chardi kala, ever-rising spirits, and then three words: sarbat da bhala. The good of all. Not the good of Sikhs, or of this room. Everyone. After all that memory, the last thing asked for is the well-being of the whole world. Then comes the shout. Bole so nihal: whoever says it is blessed. And the answer, sat sri akal: true is the timeless one. The same words many Sikhs use to say hello.
screen: `ARDAS — A HUMBLE REQUEST.` · `A PRAYER WITH A LONG MEMORY.` · `THE DAY'S OWN REQUESTS.` · `SARBAT DA BHALA — THE GOOD OF ALL.`

segments.voice: Three breaths with the bell. Stand if you can, palms together. On the first, bring to mind the people closest to you. On the second, widen it to strangers. On the third, widen it once more, to someone you find hard to wish well.
Ardas. The standing prayer: it remembers, it asks, and it ends by asking for the good of all. Fifth word.
Your line: for everyone, not just us. Those are the prayer's last words, and they leave nobody out. Day five, done.

6.title: are Sikhs Hindu or Muslim?
6.hook: the question Sikhs get asked from both sides, and the plain answer: a learner, on a path of its own
6.carry: a learner, on a path of its own
6.howItsDone: Sikhs follow the teaching of the ten Gurus and the Guru Granth Sahib, with their own initiation and gurdwaras; many explain Sikhi to friends simply as its own religion, begun by Guru Nanak in Punjab about five hundred years ago.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ardas, the standing prayer that ends with the good of all. Today, a question many Sikhs get asked, and a plain answer to it.

So, are Sikhs a kind of Hindu? Or a kind of Muslim? Sikhs hear both, sometimes in the same week. Surveys in the United States have found many people guessing Sikhism is a branch of Islam; others assume it's part of Hinduism. The plain answer is neither. And why people mix it up turns out to be a good story.
screen: `A KIND OF HINDU?` → `A KIND OF MUSLIM?` → `THE PLAIN ANSWER: NEITHER.`

segments.voice: Start with the word. Sikh is Punjabi for a learner, a student: someone who learns from the Guru. So nobody starts out finished. The path began with Guru Nanak, born, tradition says, in 1469, in Punjab, and grew through ten Gurus over about two hundred years. It has its own scripture, its own initiation, which you met on day four, and its own houses of worship. So it's a religion of its own, not a branch of another. Why the mix-up? Nanak was born into a Hindu family and grew up among Hindu and Muslim neighbors. His companion on years of travel, Mardana, was a Muslim musician. Sikh scripture uses names for God that both neighbors used, and it even holds hymns by holy poets born into Hindu and Muslim families, beside the Gurus' own. Sharing words isn't the same as being the same. Then there's the turban and the beard, which people who don't know often read as Muslim, and that mistake hasn't always been harmless. The first words Nanak is remembered saying, as his mission began, were: there is no Hindu, there is no Muslim. Some hear in that: beneath the labels, everyone is made by the one. Others hear a challenge: nobody was living up to the name they carried. Either way, it put no one down. It was a starting point.

story.title: the thread that wouldn't break
story.text: A boy of about eleven sits in front of the family priest, guests all around, on the day he's meant to receive a sacred cotton thread over his shoulder. The priest reaches for it, and the boy asks: what is this for, and will it last? He isn't mocking anyone. He says he'd gladly wear a thread spun from compassion and contentment, knotted with self-control and twisted with truth: one that never breaks, never gets dirty, never burns and is never lost. The boy was Nanak.

7.title: the symbol on the flag
7.hook: the symbol on the flag outside the gurdwara, on car windows and pendants: what each piece means
7.carry: the inner and the outer, held together
7.howItsDone: The Khanda appears on the Nishan Sahib, the saffron or blue flag that flies on a tall pole at gurdwaras; at Vaisakhi many gurdwaras renew the flag and the pole's cloth, and Sikhs celebrate the harvest and the Khalsa's founding with Nagar Kirtan processions.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sikh, a learner on a path of its own. Six words so far: Waheguru, langar, the turban, Panj Pyare, Ardas, Sikh. Today, the seventh.
screen: `WAHEGURU · LANGAR · THE TURBAN · PANJ PYARE · ARDAS · SIKH`

segments.voice: It's on the flag outside the gurdwara. On car window stickers, pendants, gates, phone cases and forearms. A circle, a straight double-edged sword through the middle, and two curved swords wrapped around the outside. Plenty of people could draw it from memory. Fewer could say what each piece means.
screen: `ON THE FLAG. ON THE CAR. ON THE ARM.` → `A CIRCLE, AND THREE SWORDS.` → `WHAT EACH PIECE MEANS.`

segments.voice: It's called the Khanda, after the sword in the middle. A khanda is a straight, double-edged sword, the very kind of blade that stirred the water at the first initiation, with the five from day four. Sikhs often read its two edges as the power to cut truth from falsehood. Around it, the circle, the chakkar. It was once a real steel ring, thrown in battle, but in the emblem it's read as the one with no beginning and no end, like the kara on the wrist. Then the two curved swords on the outside. They're usually read as miri and piri: the outer life and the inner life, the world and the spirit, held together. The sixth Guru, Guru Hargobind, wore two swords to say exactly that. So at the center there's no crown and no face: just a blade that cuts lies. The flag it flies on, the Nishan Sahib, is saffron or blue, on a tall pole, so anyone, from far off, can find shelter and a meal. And at Vaisakhi, the spring harvest festival and the day the five stood up, many gurdwaras lower the flag, wash the pole and dress it in fresh cloth.
screen: `THE KHANDA — A DOUBLE-EDGED SWORD.` · `THE CIRCLE — NO BEGINNING, NO END.` · `MIRI AND PIRI — WORLD AND SPIRIT.` · `THE FLAG SAYS: SHELTER AND A MEAL.`

The Khanda. A double-edged sword, a circle without end, and two swords for world and spirit. Seventh word: a week's worth.

story.title: two swords, not one
story.text: A boy of eleven is about to become the sixth Guru, just after his father's death. At the ceremony, tradition says, he's offered the old signs of the role, and he asks for two swords instead. He straps on both. One, he says, is for miri, the world: protecting people, standing up to wrong. The other is for piri, the spirit. He was Guru Hargobind, and his two swords still curve around the outside of the Khanda.
